points: Training data: the examples an AI system learns its patterns from before it is used.
Too little data on a group means the AI learns that group's pattern poorly, so its judgments about that group are less accurate — it can misjudge them more often.
8.marking: 1 mark each. Accept any wording that says the AI learns from examples, and that under-represented groups are judged less accurately.

points: From the data (either): insufficient data on certain attributes; or past discriminatory tendencies reflected in the data.
From the way it is built (any one): an inappropriate choice of variables; a proxy variable that indirectly stands in for a protected attribute; the design of the model itself.
9.marking: 2 marks each side: 1 for naming the cause, 1 for saying how it leads to biased judgments.

points: Surveillance through face-recognition technology: cameras in public spaces can identify and track individuals.
Mass collection of personal data: large amounts of online behaviour data are collected and analysed.
10.marking: 1 mark for naming each issue, 1 for the explanation.

points: XAI: technology that makes it possible for humans to understand why an AI made a particular judgment.
If the process is opaque, nobody can verify whether the result is correct — a right answer by chance cannot be told apart from a wrong one, and an unfair decision cannot be found or challenged.
11.marking: 2 marks for the definition; 3 for the explanation, which must mention verification.

points: The developer, the user and the operator.

Responsibility is the roles and duties of each party — who does what, and who answers when a judgment is wrong. Accountability is being answerable for the AI's decisions: knowing who can be held to account, according to those roles. Accountability is one of the four principles.
12.marking: 1 mark for the three parties; 3 for a clear difference, not two restated definitions of the same thing.

13: Fairness — not unjustly discriminating against any particular person or group — e.g. a hiring AI evaluating fairly regardless of gender
Transparency — showing the decision-making process and inner workings clearly — e.g. telling users in plain language how the AI decides
Privacy protection — handling personal information appropriately — e.g. not using collected data for another purpose
Accountability — being answerable for the AI's decisions — e.g. someone answers when a diagnostic result is wrong

14.model: Algorithmic bias arises because an AI learns its patterns from training data. If that data is biased — for example, it contains too little data on certain groups, or it reflects past discrimination — the AI reproduces the same bias in its judgments. Bias can also enter through the way the system is built, such as a proxy variable that stands in for a protected attribute. It can be reduced by checking the training data for missing or unfair patterns and testing the AI's results across different groups, which applies the principle of fairness; and by making the decision-making process visible, for example with explainable AI, which applies the principle of transparency and lets people find and correct unfair decisions.
points: Cause: the AI learns from training data (1)
Biased or insufficient data is reproduced in its judgments, with an example (1)
A second source: past discrimination in data, or proxy variable / variable choice (1)
Reduction through fairness: check data, test results across groups (1)
Reduction through transparency: show the decision process / XAI (1)
Links the measures back to the cause, so the answer is an analysis, not a list (1)
14.marking: Six points, one mark each. A list of the four principles with no link to bias earns no more than 2.

points: Most likely cause: the training data reflected past bias — e.g. past hiring decisions that favoured one gender, or too little data on the other (2)
One measure, justified by a principle: check the data and test results for each gender (fairness), or make the reasons visible (transparency), or name who answers for the system (accountability) (2)
15.marking: Accept any reasonable measure that is tied to a named principle.

points: Benefit: attendance recorded automatically and quickly; saves teachers' time (1)
Privacy concern: students' faces are personal data; they can be tracked, or the data used for another purpose (1)
Responsibility: either answer can earn the marks, if reasoned — the school chose and operates it; the company built it and chose its data (2)
16.marking: The book allows more than one view on responsibility; mark the reasoning, not the side chosen.

points: A real, sourced case — not recalled from memory without a source (1)
The group affected (1)
The data that might have caused it, linked to biased or insufficient training data (2)
Names one use (1)
A concrete rule (1)
Justified by a named principle of AI ethics (1)

19: (1) B — a qubit uses superposition to be a mixture of 0 and 1 at the same time

(2) A classical bit holds one state, 0 or 1. A qubit uses superposition, so it can be 0 and 1 at the same time; this is what lets quantum computers speed up computations that are difficult for traditional computers.
20: (2) Edge computing processes the data on the vehicle itself, immediately, instead of sending it to the cloud. Even a 0.1-second delay could cause an accident, so deciding on board makes the vehicle faster to react and therefore safer.
21: (2) Connected layers of units (artificial neurons) — an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer — whose connection weights change during training.
22: (2) AI recognises the voice, understands the command and carries it out. Examples: Siri, Google Assistant.
23: (1) B — predicting harvest timing and detecting pests and diseases
(2) AI analyses data and images from the fields to predict when to harvest and to detect pests and crop diseases early.
24: (1) B — it is unclear how the AI reached its judgment; option C is a different caution, copyright

(2) Black box: it is unclear how the AI reached its judgment, so its result is hard to verify. Rights issues: using copyrighted works as training data raises the question of whether the owners' rights are respected.
